sentences.text:
The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954
(Pfa Act), alleging that the accused has violated the provisions of the Pfa Act and Rules.

The
acc
used mani Ram is stated to be the vendor-cum-proprietor of M/s. Aggarwal Sweet India, from where the food article, that is, 'Boondi Laddu' was lifted for sampling.

2. As per the complaint, on 28.02.2004, food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI) Sanjeev Kumar Gupta and Food Assistant (FA) Brahma Nand under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. Harish Kumar Ahuja reached along with their staff at the premises in question where the accused was found conducting the business of various food articles, which were lying stored/exposed for sale for human consumption.
The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of Boondi Laddu from the vendor lying in an open tray (ready for sale) bearing no label declaration, to which he agreed.
The sample was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.

Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the Notice as per Form-VI,
panchnama, etc.
The price of sample was paid to the vendor.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.

Vide report dated 12.03.2004, the PA found the sample to be adulterated on the ground that the total dye content of synthetic colour used exceeded the prescribed maximum In Re vs Mani Ram on 5 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144865504/
1 limit'.

sentences.text: Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by the FI.
After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.

The complaint was then filed in the court by FI on 29.06.2004 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(j) and (m) of PFA Act as well as Rules 28, 29 and 30 of PFA Rules, as punishable section 7/16(1A) of PFA Act.
3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused was summoned vide order dated 29.06.2004.
Upon appearance, the accused moved an application thereby exercising his right under section 13(2) PFA Act to get the second counterpart of the sample analysed by the Central Food Laboratory (CFL).
However, the accused made statement on 16.08.2005 that he was not inclined to send the sample for analysis to CFL and wanted to withdraw his application.
The said application was thus dismissed as withdrawn.
4. The matter was then listed for pre-charge evidence, wherein the complainant examined PW-1 FI Sanjeev Kumar.

On the basis of his deposition, charge was framed against the accused on 01.09.2010 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a), (j) and (m) of PFA Act, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.

At the trial, the witness already examined in pre-charge stage was recalled for further cross-examination in post-charge stage and additionally, the prosecution examined PW-2 Sh.
Harish Kumar Ahuja (SDM/LHA) and PW-3 FA Brahmanand in post- charge stage.

5. At the trial, PW-1, PW-2 and PW-3 who were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings, deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 28.02.2004 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity,
expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 1500 gms of Boondi Laddu taken from an open tray, payment of price of sample, breaking the commodity into smallest possible pieces using a clean and dry steel spoon, mixing it using the said spoon, dividing them by putting them equally in three clean and dry sample glass bottles, adding 40 drops of formalin as preservative, separately sealing, packing and marking the sample bottles and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.

They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex.
PW-1/A, Notice as per Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B and Panchnama Ex. PW-1/C.

On the next working day,
that is 01.03.2004, one counterpart of sample along with Memo as per Form-VII were sent to PA for analysis vide PA Receipt Ex.
PW-1 /D and remaining two counterparts with copy of Memos were deposited with LHA/SDM vide receipt Ex. PW-1/E.
PA report Ex. PW-1/F was received and upon direction of SDM/LHA, investigation was carried out by PW-1.
He sent letter Ex. PW-1/G to the STO and received its reply.
He also received reply Ex. PW-1/H from the accused.

After completion of the investigation, sanction/consent Ex. PW-1/J was taken from the Director PFA and the complaint Ex.
PW-1/K was filed in the court.

After this, intimation letter Ex. PW-1/L with copy of PA report was sent to the accused through registered post vide postal receipt Ex. PW-1/M and was also personally delivered to the accused against proper endorsement.
These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence counsel wherein they denied that the sample proceedings were not proper or that the accused had been falsely implicated.

sentences.text: Statement of the accused under section 313 CrPC was recorded on 23.03.2016 wherein he denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
He accepted the proceedings dated 28.02.2004, though claimed that sampling method was not proper and the sample bottles were not cleaned despite his request.
He however did not lead any evidence in defence.

7. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that he has not been able to rebut the findings in the PA report dated 12.03.2004.
It is pointed out that the accused has failed to exercise his right under section 13(2) PFA Act and failed to get the sample analysed from CFL.
It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony.
8. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various missing links in the testimony of witnesses.

Ld.
Counsel as questioned the PA report on the ground that there has been an unexplained delay of three days in signing the report, relying upon the judgements titled as Delhi Administration v. Amar Chand [2012 (3) JCC 1930] and State of Gujrat v. Vishramdas Virumal [2005 (1) FAC 48].

entities.text: Delhi Administration v. Amar Chand [2012 (3) JCC 1930]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: State of Gujrat v. Vishramdas Virumal [2005 (1) FAC 48]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is further submitted that Tartrazine is not a harmful colouring matter as its use is permitted in many food articles.

Ld. Counsel has also submitted that there were violations of various provisions of PFA Rules during sample proceedings in as much as the spoon and sample bottles used were not made clean and dry, and also that no independent public witness was joined in the proceedings.
It is finally contended that the laboratory in which the sample was analysed and the testing method were not notified under the Rules and therefore the prosecution is bad in law.
9. I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused and have carefully perused the material available on record.
10. It is to be understood that the charge framed against the accused is for violation of section 2(ia)(a), (j) and (m) of the PFA Act read with Rule 30 of PFA Rules with respect to 'adulteration'.

Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature,
substance or quality which it purported or represented to be.
Section 2(ia)(j) specifically deals with colouring matter which is present other than prescribed or is present beyond the prescribed limits of variability.

Section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act deals with situation where the quality or purity of an article falls below the prescribed standard or its constituents are present in quantities not within the prescribed limits of variability.
11. To begin with, it is seen that the accused has not exercised his right under section 13(2) PFA Act for getting the sample analysed through CFL.
This is not a case where the accused has raised a defence that he was not served with copy of PA report or intimation letter.
Record rather shows that the said letter and report were sent to the accused through post and he was also served with the same personally.

For that matter, the accused had also moved an application under section 13(2)
PFA Act but chose to withdraw it on 16.08.2005.

Therefore, it cannot be said that this right of the In Re vs Mani Ram on 5 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144865504/
3 accused got frustrated due to any act or omission of the prosecution/complainant.
Even in his statement under section 313 CrPC, the accused never took stand that intimation letter with PA report had not been received by him.
The accused has himself forgiven his right and thus, he cannot say that he was prejudiced.
The accused has deliberately and voluntarily forgiven his right under section 13(2) of the Act.
It is not a case where the right of the accused got frustrated due to any delay in filing the prosecution.
The nature of synthetic colours is such that no period of delay would change its nature, quality or quantity.
Such argument is liable to be rejected.
12. The commodity in the present case is Boondi Laddu which falls in the category of sweets.

The article does not fall in any of the items of Appendix-B to the PFA Rules and is thus treated as "proprietary food"
within the meaning of Rule 37-A of PFA Rules.
As per clause (e) of Rule 37-A, such food article shall not contain food additives other than those prescribed under the Rules for that food and/or category of foods.
13. As per Rule 23 of PFA Rules, addition of a colouring matter to any article of food except as specifically permitted by the Rules is prohibited.
Rule 28 provides the details of colours permitted for use.
Tartrazine, as found to be used in the present case, is one of the permitted colours for use in food.
Rule 29 enlists the foods in which synthetic colours are permitted.
Clause (b) of this list would show that it mentions 'sweets' as the food in which synthetic colours are permitted.
However, Rule 30 provides the maximum limit upto which permitted synthetic colours can be used in permissible food articles.
It provides that the maximum permissible limit for such colour is 100 ppm (parts per million) of the final food for consumption.
The food article "sweets" does not fall in clause (c) of Rule 29 where this limit is upto 200 ppm.

14. The present case is based on the findings of PA as given in report Ex. PW-1/F that has found the presence of the synthetic colouring matter Tartrazine in the sample analysed upto the extent of 226.52 ppm as against the permitted limit of 100 ppm.
15. Well, there is nothing for the court to disbelieve the PA report wherein synthetic colour tartrazine has been detected in the food article beyond the prescribed limits.
Report of chemical expert is admissible in evidence under section 293 CrPC without formal examination of such expert.

As far as this report is concerned, the contents and findings therein have not been disputed by the defence, though it is claimed that such findings are wrong on account of incorrect sampling proceedings.
It is nowhere the defence of the accused that there was some mistake in the report or that the food was not analysed properly or that some invalid method had been adopted by the PA.
The accused never applied to cross- examine the PA when this option was available to him under section 293 CrPC, so as to question her on her report or to seek any clarification.

It is not the defence of the accused that no colour was detected, or was detected wrongly, or that any such colour was a result of natural environment or the food article having been exposed to natural environment.
No suggestion to this effect was given to any witness during cross-examination.
No such defence was raised by the accused in his statement under section 313 CrPC.

sentences.text: Rather the accused had taken a stand during the trial by putting specific suggestions to all the three PWs that the tray, spoon, bottles used in sample proceedings were not clean and dry and some yellow colour was sticking to them.
By taking such a stand, the accused has virtually lost his right to take a contradictory plea that the colour was within permissible range in the sample.
It is apparent that the accused has accepted the presence of excess colour in the sample, though has claimed that it was on account of wrong sampling procedure.
There was no occasion for him to allege incorrect sample proceedings if the colour was within limit.
Thus even from this angle, it is evident that the sample was having excess food colour.
17. There is no merit in the contention that Tartrazine is a permissible colour and no prejudice would be caused to any customer.
As per section 19(1) of PFA Act, it shall be no defence that the food article sold had not caused any prejudice to the purchaser.
Such colour is permissible only upto certain limits and such limits cannot be rendered nullified on the pretext that no harm has been caused.
No person is allowed to use any quantity of such permitted food colours.
18. All the PWs have corroborated the stand of each other on facts.
All deposed about attempt made to join public persons as witnesses.
All deposed about steps taken during sample proceedings.
There is no contradiction in their statements that can be said to be material enough so as to go to the root of the matter.
There is nothing to disbelieve them or to shake their credibility.
It is not a case of non-compliance of any Rule or procedure.
Rather the witnesses categorically deposed about compliance of due procedure and there is nothing in their cross-examination so as to attach any falsity to their version.
19. All the three PWs deposed about use of clean and dry tray, spoon and glass bottles.
They maintained this stand even during their cross- examination.
PW-1 stated that about 3-4 kg laddus were available at the spot, and PW-2 and PW-3 maintained that there were around 2-3 kg available.
As the matter pertains to year 2004 and the witnesses were examined after about ten years, such variation is very minor in nature.

All the three witnesses in corroboration to each other deposed that the food article was weighted in a polythene bag, which the PW-3 affirmed to be in clean and dry state, before it was transferred to another clean and dry tray to be broken in small pieces and mixed with a clean and dry spoon.
All maintained that the sample bottles were clean an dry when used and denied that some yellow colour was there in/on the bottles, tray or spoon.
20. The fate of the case depends on quality of witnesses and not their quantity or designation or professions.
There is no rule of law that requires the evidence of food officials to be viewed with any suspicion.
What is required is that attempt is made to join public persons as witnesses as a matter of prudence.
The court is not oblivious of reluctance of public persons to join such legal proceedings that involves lengthy procedural formalities and strict future commitments.
But non joining of such witnesses would not negate the testimony of official witnesses when they are otherwise truthful and credit worthy and have withstood the test of cross-examination.
No motive has shown to exist giving them reason to depose falsely against the accused.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Shriram Labhaya v. MCD [1948-1997 FAC (SC) 483] has categorically held that testimony of the Food Inspector alone,
if believed, is sufficient to convict the accused and there is no requirement of independent corroboration by public persons unless the testimony suffers from fatal inconsistencies.

No such In Re vs Mani Ram on 5 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144865504/
5 inconsistency can be seen in this case.
No violation of any rule or provision has been pointed out by the defence.
21. There is no merit in the stand that the bottles/tray/spoon were not clean and dry.
All the witnesses have testified this fact on oath in court.
This fact has not been controverted by the defence, except by putting bald suggestions which have been categorically denied by the PWs.
The Ld. Counsel has failed to explain what other "positive evidence" he required from the witnesses in addition to their corroborative testimony to establish this fact.
Rather the accused has failed to lead any evidence to prove his defence that the spoon, tray or bottles were not clean and dry when used.

There is no witness examined in defence who could depose that the sample bottles or utensils or implements were not clean or dry or were contaminated with any extraneous colour as alleged by the accused.
Mere bald suggestions would not serve the purpose of the accused.

This is more so when no such stand has been taken by the accused even in his statement under section 313 CrPC.
22.
Again, there is no merit in the contention that the evidence does not show that Form-VII was sent separately by the FI.
PW-1 specifically deposed about this fact.
Even the PA receipt Ex. PW-1/D states that this form was sent separately in a sealed cover.
No questions were raised on this point at the trial and there was no cross-examination of the FI on this point.
23. Further, there is no merit in the stand of the accused that the report of PA is not reliable on the ground that the same was signed after three days.
As per the report, the sample was analysed from 05.03.2004 to 09.03.2004.
The report was signed on 12.03.2004, that is, after about three days.
Well, the court is not in a position to term such a period as "unexplained delay" particularly when no opportunity was granted to the PA to explain any such delay.
As already stated, the accused did not exercise his option to apply and cross examine the PA under section 293 CrPC.
She was the best person to explain any such delay.

Such delay can be due to vacations, leaves, administrative reasons,
official exigencies, analytical studies etc.
But when no opportunity has been given to the PA, the court cannot on hypothetical assumptions assume that the said delay has not been explained so as to negate the entire prosecution case.
No clarification on this point was sought even from the FI who had conducted the investigation.
Thus, no benefit can be given to the accused on this count.
24. Moving ahead, the defence claims that method of analysis and laboratories were not specified by the Rule-making authority and thus, prosecution was bad.
It has been argued that the prosecution was launched on 29.06.2004 on the basis of the Public Analyst's report dated 12.03.2004.
Relying upon the judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court titled Pepsico India Holdings Pvt. Ltd. v. Food Inspector [2010(2) PFA Cases 310],

entities.text: Pepsico India Holdings Pvt. Ltd. v. Food Inspector [2010(2) PFA Cases 310]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: the Ld.

Defence counsel has argued that the prosecution was bad in law and no prosecution could have been launched because Section 23, which empowered the Central Government to make rules to carry out the provisions of the Act, was amended with effect from 01.04.1976 and Sub Clause (ee) and (hh) were inserted in Clause (1A) of section 23 which included power to define/ designate laboratories competent to analyze the sample as well as define the methods of analysis to be used.

In Re vs Mani Ram on 5 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144865504/
6 25.

sentences.text: Well, if such an interpretation is to be given, then all the cases of whatever nature, of whatever ingredient and of any amount of adulteration, registered after 01.04.1976 would lead to outright dismissal en block, without going into any other evidence, on the ground that laboratories or methods have not been specified, and particularly between 01.04.1976 and 25.03.2008 on the ground that method of analysis was not specified.
But such an interpretation is not possible or plausible.

There are large number of precedents during this period where the guilty persons had been booked and convicted and their convictions and sentences upheld by the superior courts throughout the country.

26. As far as analysis by the PA and launching of the prosecution on her report is concerned it is to be seen that as per the scheme of the Act the first analysis of the sample/food product is done by the Public Analyst in terms of section 8, 11 and 13 of the Act.
The Public Analyst is appointed by the Central or State government by way of notification in the official gazette.

Unless the report of Public Analyst is superseded by that of Director, CFL, this report holds good for all purposes and remains effective and valid and can be used as evidence of the facts stated therein.
There is nothing to show that the PA Smt. Mohini Srivastava was not validly appointed as Public Analyst or could not have analyzed the sample.
No such stand was taken at the trial and PA was not sought to be cross-examined under section 293 CrPC to explain the facts.
Even her report also mentions that she had been duly appointed and this fact was never disputed at the time of trial.
27. At this stage it would be worthwhile to highlight extracts of Preface to the first edition of the DGHS Manual.

The same reads as:
"The Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954 came into effect from Ist June 1955.
Adulteration has been defined in section 2 of the PFA Act.

Under sub-clause (I) of clause (i) of section 2, it has been stated that an article of food shall be deemed to be adulterated, if the quality or purity of the article falls below the prescribed standards or its constituents are present in quantities which are in excess of the prescribed limits of variability.
The specifications prescribed for the purity of various articles of food have been given in Appendix 'B' of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules.

The analysts as well as food technologists and Analysts employed in various organisations have been using various method of tests for the determination of different components whose limits have been laid down under these rules.
As the methods adopted by Analysts are different, the results obtained may sometime differ even in the case of the same food product analysed at different food laboratories.

The Central Committee for Food Standards considered this subject in detail and desired that methods of tests as available with the various institutions like Indian Standards Institution, Directorate of Marketing and Inspection etc. be aligned and published for the guidance of Public Analysts and other analytical chemists so as to have a uniformity in the reports.

A sub- committee under the convenership of Dr. Sadgopal,
Deputy Director General Indian Standards Institution with Shri R.K. Malik, Senior Marketing Officer, Directorate of Marketing and Inspection and Shri S.N. Mitra,
Director, Central Food Laboratory, Calcutta was constituted for the purpose.

These In Re vs Mani Ram on 5 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144865504/
7 methods of tests having been recommended by the Sub-committee and approved by Central Committee for Food Standards are published for the guidance of all concerned."
28. This Manual was published in the year 1975 and its chief purpose was to lay down the methods to be employed for analysis of different food products.
As is evident from its Preface the Central Committee for Food Standards published the same so as to be the guidance for Public Analysts and Analytical Chemists to have a uniformity in the reports.

Section 3 of the PFA Act empowers the Central Government to form/constitute the above Committee, that is, Central Committee for Food Standards to advise the Central as well as the State Governments on matters arising out of administration of this Act and to carry out the other functions assigned to it under this Act.
29. Therefore, on the day of analysis of the sample in question, the Public Analyst was competent to analyze the sample and use the method she deemed fit for the purpose of analysis of the sample.

There is nothing to show that any method adopted by her was not a sure or reliable test, particularly when she was not even sought to be cross-examined by applying under section 293 CrPC on this point.
30. As far as Pepsico's case (supra) is concerned, the judgement cannot be read in isolation or selectively.
It has to be read as a whole keeping in mind the purpose and the scheme of the Act which intends to safeguard the public at large from the evil/ menace of food adulteration.

The relevant portion of the judgement relied upon by the Ld. Defence counsel reads as:
"34.

As far as Grounds 1 and 2 are concerned, the High Court was not convinced with the submission made on behalf of the appellants that in the absence of any prescribed and validated method of analysis under Section 23(1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the 1954 Act,
the report of the Public Analyst, who had used the DGHS method, could not be relied upon, especially when even the Laboratories, where the test for detection of insecticides and pesticides in an article of food could be undertaken, had not been specified.

The observation of the Division Bench of the High Court that if the submissions made on behalf of the Appellants herein were to be accepted, the mechanism of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder would come to a grinding halt, is not acceptable to us, since the same could lead to a pick and choose method to suit the prosecution.

However, in any event, the percentage of Carbofuran detected in the sample of Pepsico which was sent for examination to the Forensic Laboratory is within the tolerance limits prescribed for Sweetened Carbonated Water with effect from 17th June, 2009.

35. The High Court also misconstrued the provisions of Section 23(1-A)(ee) and (hh)
in holding that the same were basically enabling provisions and were not mandatory and could, in any event, be solved by the Central Government by framing Rules thereunder, by which specified tests to be held in designated Laboratories could be spelt out.

Consequently, the High Court also erred in holding that the non- formulation of Rules under the aforesaid provisions of the 1954 Act could not be said In Re vs Mani Ram on 5 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144865504/
8 to be fatal for the prosecution."
31. Thus, in that case, even the laboratories where the tests were to be performed for determining content of pesticides in sweetened carbonated drinks were not specified.
At that time, it was no Rule framed by the government specifying as to what quantity of pesticides was permissible.
But in the case at hand, specific Rules are there with respect to extent of use of artificial synthetic colours in sweets.
In this case, prosecution is for violation of section 2(ia)(a), (j) and (m) of the Act.
The present case would be squarely covered by the judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court titled as Prem Ballab v. State (Delhi Administration) [(1977) 1 SCC 173].

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This judgement was discussed even in Pepsico's case, but was never disturbed and was sought to be distinguished on the ground that this was dealing with colouring matter (as in the present case) and not with pesticides in carbonated water.
But when the present case is also with respect to colouring matter and not pesticides in carbonated water, the ruling in Pepsico's case would not help the accused.
32. The judgements relied upon by the accused would also not come to his rescue.

The judgements titled as Mangal Singh v. State [1976(II) PFA Cases 139], Hans Raj v. State of Punjab [1980(II) PFA Cases 396], State of Himachal Pradesh v. Kamlesh Chand [2002(2) FAC 315], State of Orrisa v.
Rabindra Sahu [2006(1) FAC 200], State of MP v. Uma Shankar [2007 FAJ 478], State of Maharashtra v. Raj Karan [1988(II) PFA Cases 156], Delhi Administration v. Suraj [Crl. A No.
192/2005, Delhi High Court, dated 10.12.2013] would apply to their own set of facts, circumstances and evidence where it was found that some rule was not complied with.

None of the said judgements would apply to the present case so as to give any benefit to the accused.
33. No other stand has been taken by the accused at the trial or during the arguments advanced.

34. The case in hand would be covered under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act as there is evidence to show that it was not of the nature, substance or quality which it is "purported" to be as per PFA Rules,
under section 2(ia)
(j) as there is presence of colour which is in excess of the prescribed limits in this article, and under section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act as the constituent of colour is present in quantities not within the prescribed limits.
Violation of section 2(ia)(j) is punishable under section 16(1A) and violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) is punishable under section 16(i)(a) of PFA Act.

But being graver offence,
his conviction can be under section 16(1A) of PFA Act.

sentences.text: Having said so, it can be said that the complainant / prosecution has been able to establish its case and prove the guilt of the accused beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt.

It has been proved that the accused had sold adulterated food in violation of section 2(ia)(a), (j) and (m) of PFA Act read with Rules 28, 29 and 30 of PFA Rules, and has committed the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) of PFA Act.

opennyai_summary.facts: On the basis of his deposition, charge was framed against the accused on 01.09.2010 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a), (j) and (m) of PFA Act, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
10. It is to be understood that the charge framed against the accused is for violation of section 2(ia)(a), (j) and (m) of the PFA Act read with Rule 30 of PFA Rules with respect to 'adulteration'.
Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature,
substance or quality which it purported or represented to be.
This is not a case where the accused has raised a defence that he was not served with copy of PA report or intimation letter.
Even in his statement under section 313 CrPC, the accused never took stand that intimation letter with PA report had not been received by him.
The accused has himself forgiven his right and thus, he cannot say that he was prejudiced.
The accused has deliberately and voluntarily forgiven his right under section 13(2) of the Act.
It is not a case where the right of the accused got frustrated due to any delay in filing the prosecution.
It is nowhere the defence of the accused that there was some mistake in the report or that the food was not analysed properly or that some invalid method had been adopted by the PA.
The accused never applied to cross- examine the PA when this option was available to him under section 293 CrPC, so as to question her on her report or to seek any clarification.
It is not the defence of the accused that no colour was detected, or was detected wrongly, or that any such colour was a result of natural environment or the food article having been exposed to natural environment.
By taking such a stand, the accused has virtually lost his right to take a contradictory plea that the colour was within permissible range in the sample.
Thus even from this angle, it is evident that the sample was having excess food colour.
As per section 19(1) of PFA Act, it shall be no defence that the food article sold had not caused any prejudice to the purchaser.
Such colour is permissible only upto certain limits and such limits cannot be rendered nullified on the pretext that no harm has been caused.
No person is allowed to use any quantity of such permitted food colours.
It is not a case of non-compliance of any Rule or procedure.
There is no rule of law that requires the evidence of food officials to be viewed with any suspicion.
What is required is that attempt is made to join public persons as witnesses as a matter of prudence.
The court is not oblivious of reluctance of public persons to join such legal proceedings that involves lengthy procedural formalities and strict future commitments.
But non joining of such witnesses would not negate the testimony of official witnesses when they are otherwise truthful and credit worthy and have withstood the test of cross-examination.
No motive has shown to exist giving them reason to depose falsely against the accused.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Shriram Labhaya v. MCD [1948-1997 FAC (SC) 483] has categorically held that testimony of the Food Inspector alone,
if believed, is sufficient to convict the accused and there is no requirement of independent corroboration by public persons unless the testimony suffers from fatal inconsistencies.
Rather the accused has failed to lead any evidence to prove his defence that the spoon, tray or bottles were not clean and dry when used.
There is no witness examined in defence who could depose that the sample bottles or utensils or implements were not clean or dry or were contaminated with any extraneous colour as alleged by the accused.
Well, the court is not in a position to term such a period as "unexplained delay" particularly when no opportunity was granted to the PA to explain any such delay.
She was the best person to explain any such delay.
Such delay can be due to vacations, leaves, administrative reasons,
official exigencies, analytical studies etc.
But when no opportunity has been given to the PA, the court cannot on hypothetical assumptions assume that the said delay has not been explained so as to negate the entire prosecution case.
It has to be read as a whole keeping in mind the purpose and the scheme of the Act which intends to safeguard the public at large from the evil/ menace of food adulteration.
The present case would be squarely covered by the judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court titled as Prem Ballab v. State (Delhi Administration) [(1977) 1 SCC 173].
The judgements titled as Mangal Singh v. State [1976(II) PFA Cases 139], Hans Raj v. State of Punjab [1980(II) PFA Cases 396], State of Himachal Pradesh v. Kamlesh Chand [2002(2) FAC 315], State of Orrisa v.
Rabindra Sahu [2006(1) FAC 200], State of MP v. Uma Shankar [2007 FAJ 478], State of Maharashtra v. Raj Karan [1988(II) PFA Cases 156], Delhi Administration v. Suraj [Crl. A No.
192/2005, Delhi High Court, dated 10.12.2013] would apply to their own set of facts, circumstances and evidence where it was found that some rule was not complied with.
